page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: Anomers are the two cyclic hemiacetal forms
of a sugar that differ only in the
That carbon is C₁ in an aldose and C₂ in a
ketose. It is called the anomeric carbon.
steps.why: When the ring closes, the carbonyl carbon becomes a new stereocentre, so two forms are possible and they differ at that one carbon only. Naming which carbon it is, C₁ for an aldose and C₂ for a ketose, is what the answer key asks for.
common_mistakes: Saying anomers differ at any carbon atom. They differ only at the anomeric carbon.
Defining anomers for the open chain form. Anomers exist only in the cyclic form, because the ring creates the new centre.
steps.memory_tip: Anomers differ at one carbon only, the one the ring closed on.
steps.margin_note: Name the carbon, C₁ or C₂. A definition without it is usually half this mark.

steps.label: Example
lines: In α-D-glucose the –OH at C₁ lies on the
same side as the –OH that closed the ring.
In β-D-glucose it lies on the opposite
In water the two interconvert, which is
steps.why: Glucose is the standard example because both anomers can be crystallised separately and both are stable enough to measure. Mutarotation is the direct consequence: in solution the ring opens and closes, so a pure anomer changes into the equilibrium mixture and its optical rotation drifts to a fixed value.
common_mistakes: Calling α and β glucose enantiomers. Enantiomers are mirror images; anomers differ at one carbon only.
Writing that the two forms cannot interconvert. In water they do, through the open chain form.
steps.memory_tip: α and β glucose are the standard pair, and mutarotation is the change between them.
steps.margin_note: One named pair earns this mark. Adding the word mutarotation costs nothing and shows the reason.

insider_note: One carbon is the whole answer: the anomeric carbon, C₁ in an aldose. Give α and β glucose as the example and add mutarotation if there is a line to spare.
